list.name: Rìoghachd Dia-thìr
list.note: The council of the rising made itself a kingdom, crowned Niall by Macha's rite, drew the shires on the humans' lines and struck its own coin with coal-dust in the seal. The vein is failing under it, and Mairead is its fourth ruler. Its ruler at the close of the age: Mairead, ruler of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Told of in: Rìoghachd Dia-thìr declared (SE 2); The council of the kingdom seated (SE 2); Niall crowned (SE 3); The shires drawn (SE 3); The maoir appointed (SE 4).

list.name: Tional nan Tuathach
list.note: The Tuathaich householders meet at Caol mhòr under a speaker they choose, and keep minutes, schools, a register of the pit dead and granaries the kingdom never licensed and never shut. Tional nan Tuathach has no standing in law and has never asked for any. Its speaker is Daniel Frayne of Muileann leathan. Its ruler at the close of the age: Daniel Frayne, speaker of Tional nan Tuathach. Told of in: The Tuathaich homeland fixed (SE 1); The boundary stones set (SE 1); The Moot at Caol mhòr (SE 2); Walter Hale dies (SE 33); The Moot's pit register (SE 41); Mary Coyle lays down the chair (SE 55).

1.note: A strait harbour of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd na Cloiche. A small harbour town and the seat of the greatest house of Òrd na Cloiche, a low stone hall behind the harbour with Òrd na Cloiche's own mark cut plain over the door and nothing of the state's arms on it. In the twenty-first year the order rebuilt the house at its own cost and raised a low tower over its western gable, and hung in it a bell cast, the priests said, from coin given by every ship that had put in at the harbour and come home again. It is not a large bell, nor heard much past the town walls, but the town needed nothing heard past them: from that year the bell rang the hours, the market opened by it, and the harbour court and the fair court both sat by it, until within a year nobody in the town reckoned the time any other way. Known for Lia Fàil's bell that rings the hours. Told of in: The house of the Stone at Caol leathan (SE 21); Lia Fàil's house at Caol leathan rebuilt (SE 21).

5.note: A grove village of Tional nan Tuathach. A small inland town of the north, where the Pike family had ground grain since before An Dealachadh and the smith Joseph Marlow kept his forge. When the humans' coin was cried down in the fifth year, half the town brought its dead coin to Marlow, and he melted it and cast it into ploughshares and sold them back at the cost of the charcoal; the first furrow of that spring was cut with one of them by the last day of am Màrt. Walter Hale walked ten miles through snow to see it. The Tuathaich sang of Marlow after, that he turned the king's silence into iron and the iron into bread. Tional nan Tuathach took seed oats from the town's mill on credit in the first hungry year. Marlow's son Harry went from the forge to a shipwright's yard at Cuan shean, and sent his wage home each year; Agnes Pike, who opened the byre school at Doire ghlas, was a miller's daughter of the town. Known for Joseph Marlow's ploughshares. Told of in: Seed oats taken from the Doire mhin mill on credit (SE 1); Joseph Marlow's ploughshares (SE 6); Joseph Marlow's first ploughshare (SE 6); Marlow's charge fixed at the price of the charcoal (SE 6); Harry Marlow promised to a Cuan shean yard (SE 6); Joseph Marlow's song first sung at Doire mhin (SE 6).

8.note: A hill-fort of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The Dùn thais of the west coast, within a morning's ride of Ros bheag; there are two towns of the name, and the record keeps them apart as west and east. Its fishermen settled salvage among themselves by custom until a wrecked raider's hulk driven ashore proved too rich a prize for custom to divide, and in the thirty-seventh year the town was granted a court of the sea of its own to judge salvage and wreck along its shore. At its first sitting, held on the strand, the court awarded the hulk whole to the crews who drove it aground. For ten years the royal record confused its court with the eastern town's market, until Tormod Pinn marked the two west and east in the forty-eighth year. Known for the court of the sea. Told of in: Dùn thais in the west (SE 37); Dùn thais in the west granted a sea court (SE 38); The royal record confuses the two Dùn thais (SE 38); Tormod Pinn marks the two Dùn thais west and east (SE 48).

9.note: A large village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. River-island village with a landing. Its church is of Eaglais nan Tuathach. A Tuathaich fishing harbour of the far north coast; boats were promised from its country to the second Fleadh na Mara at Cnoc ghorm. In the seventieth year, when the east-coast boats came north to the grounds the licence law kept for them and crowded the Tuathaich boats off the grounds nearest home, its boats took to the deep water beyond the northern isles, which no boat of that coast had fished in living memory for its roughness and the distance a crew had to keep from land. Two were lost the first year and none after, and before the next season was out its catch had passed Caol mhòr's. Known for the deep water beyond the northern isles. Told of in: Inis mhin's boats (SE 70); Inis mhin's boats pass Caol mhòr's own catch (SE 70).

12.note: A ford village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. A town of the eastern hills by a ford where its river fishers still bless their nets, whose Seann Spioradan house keeps the oldest folk rite on the island. Copper was found in the hills behind it in the sixtieth year, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean opened a working within the season with men laid off from An Sloc Mòr's thinning galleries. The house gave the copper no blessing, its keeper telling Comhairle nam Mèinnean's factor that copper dug for a wage was copper dug like any other stone. By the second summer the town had built a street of new stone houses for the miners on the slope above the ford and named it, before the last house had a roof, for the pit they had come from, Sràid an t-Sluic; the miners kept small lumps of An Sloc Mòr's coal among their goods, and the house's keeper told the council a street named for another town's mountain risked forgetting the ground it stood on. Known for the copper, and Sràid an t-Sluic. Told of in: The copper at Àth fhiadhaich (SE 60); Àth fhiadhaich's copper-town (SE 61); The street named for An Sloc Mòr (SE 61).

18.note: A large village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. A town of the east coast, past the last of the shires An Crùn garrisoned closely, below which the Abhainn chaol meets the sea. The houses of Na Seann Spioradan there had never had a hall of their own, only the hearth of whichever family kept the year's rite. In the twenty-second year forty households raised a common hall in a single season, working the stone by day, and roofed it before the first frost; it holds no image or carving, only two hearths. From the next year the hall sent an Leabharlann a copy of its naming every year, a little longer each time. In the sixty-eighth and sixty-ninth years the herring did not come to the grounds off the river mouth, and the town's boats went north. Known for the ancestors' hall. Told of in: The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn (SE 22); The hall raised at Seann Dunn (SE 22); Gormshuil's visit to the first naming (SE 22); An Leabharlann's offer to Seann Dunn (SE 22); Nine generations named at Seann Dunn (SE 22); The Seann Dunn list first copied to an Leabharlann (SE 23).

19.note: A town of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The capital held Comhairle na Rìoghachd from the second year of the age, seated at a table too large for the room that held it, and every warrant, ruling and refusal of the kingdom went out from it. In the first summer the disbanded companies waited in its market square to be stood down, and sixty-one company rolls were carried into the vaults under the counting-house and bricked in. Niall was crowned here in the third year, Brìghde in the twenty-second and Eòghan in the twenty-eighth, and Mairead in the fifty-eighth; the bells of Òrd Mhacha rang a day and a night for Niall's death. The mint struck Bonn na Rìoghachd here from the fifth year, Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn kept its low grey office here, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean sat here until the twenty-seventh year, when it went to Cathair mhòr. The guild court heard the indentures and the yards' protests in its chambers. A second census was locked in the council's keeping-room in the thirty-third year and never aired. By the end of the age the lamps of its poorer wards burned shorter hours than the council's lighting order required, for want of coal at the price the order was written for. Known for the council's table, the mint, and the crownings. Told of in: The Severance companies stood down (SE 1); Fearchar mac Raghnaill's plea that his company's roll be kept (SE 1); The disbanded companies' rolls kept, not burned (SE 1); Ailean's list of the chests begun (SE 1); The war-vault sealed at Cathair dhearg (SE 1); The companies wait on their packs in the market square (SE 1).

20.note: A hill village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig. A river town of the north-central country, heart of Òrd an t-Seabhaig's houses, whose altars answered to no custodian above them. In the sixth year the houses round it wrote to Seann Skell that Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's written order was handsome and not needed. The shire's arms carried a plain white billet from the fourth year for no reason any clerk could give, until the thirty-sixth, when a delegation of Òrd an t-Seabhaig asked for a hawk, and the maor broke the old die and pressed a white hawk among twelve crescents. An obelisk of unread script stands near it, which Una copied stroke by stroke in the thirty-second year and the council fenced against the cattle; its marks were laid beside those of Colbh Cnoc chiar and Calbh Cnoc ghorm by the students of Caol shean. By the forty-sixth year its river quays took in more grain in a season than the granaries of Cathair mhòr showed for a year. Known for Òrd an t-Seabhaig's country, the hawk on the seal, and Carragh Cnoc bheag. Told of in: The Hawk houses refuse (SE 6); Òrd an t-Seabhaig' letter of refusal (SE 6); The Hawk river port of Cnoc bheag (SE 46); The Hawk given a place (SE 47).

22.note: A village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Headland village with a landing. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. A town of the south where the droves from Muileann fhionn came down to market and where the fair-wardens grazed the fair's horses on rising ground outside the walls. In the twenty-third year the wardens called an old custom of arms Còmhrag Ceann leathan, and fought it on that field, drawing men from every vein-town within two days' walk; Calum Ruadh of Muileann chrom won it, took a year's wages and the right to bear arms, and four inn-keepers who had built new houses for the crowd kept his table free. Two men died in the first and six in the thirty-sixth year, and the wardens refused the custodians' petition to end it within the hour; An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn pitched on the trampled ground a week after the six burials. Slighe a' Ghuail reached the town the same season and its quays spread half a mile past the old gate. Ealasaid nic Coinnich of Àth ghlas won it in the forty-fifth year and did not fight again; edged iron was banned from the ring in the fifty-fourth. By the fifty-seventh year its coal quays stood half idle and the wardens raised the gate-price. Known for Còmhrag Ceann leathan. Told of in: Ceann leathan's inns (SE 23); The dead of the first Còmhrag buried (SE 23); The right to bear arms entered on the shire's roll (SE 23); The fair-wardens' free table (SE 23); Calum Ruadh walks home alone (SE 23); The custodians' petition against Còmhrag Ceann leathan is refused (SE 36).

23.note: A town of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's offices in the stone house of Mac Ùisdein; the market cross. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The mountain town of Taigh Mhic Ùisdein, whose family had held an overseer's post under the humans at An Sloc Mòr. Uisdean mac Ùisdein came from it to the capital in the eleventh year to take Cead an t-Sluic Mhòir, and in the twentieth year the house raised a market cross at its own cost, cut on all four faces with its name, and moved the wool and coal markets to its foot. Comhairle nam Mèinnean moved its clerks here in the twenty-seventh year, into rooms above the wool market, and set down that its surveys should be kept in its own presses and not sent to an Leabharlann. The house built its stone hall of spoil-stone in the thirtieth year and feasted Comann nan Gualadairean in it. After Sireadh na Dàrna Fèithe the house let the hall to Comhairle nam Mèinnean in the fifty-second year, and Catrìona nic Neacail hung her one sheet of the vein on its chamber wall in the fifty-sixth. Known for Taigh Mhic Ùisdein, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean's presses. Told of in: The market cross at Cathair mhòr (SE 20); The Mine Board at Cathair mhòr (SE 27); The stone house of Mac Ùisdein (SE 30); The house of Mac Ùisdein sells half (SE 52); Comhairle nam Mèinnean leaves the survey unrolled (SE 26); Ruairidh mac Ailein signs the receipt (SE 26); The survey filed and shown to no one (SE 26); Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerks move to Cathair mhòr (SE 27).

24.note: A headland harbour of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig. A fishing town of the north-central coast. In the twenty-fourth year it gave over its whole spring to a dock long enough to take three grain-ships abreast, for Oirthir an t-Seabhaig had begun to send its barley and oats down by water rather than by cart. Òrd an t-Seabhaig blessed the dock and asked a tithe of its dues; the shire's factor haggled them down to a twentieth and paid it, and has paid it every quarter since, so that the clerks of the town call the due simply Òrd an t-Seabhaig's and few of them can say why a fishing town owes a grain due to a bird that flies inland. Northern boats that landed fish at the new dock paid the same twentieth out of Tional nan Tuathach's harbour purse, which Mary Coyle raised in Tional nan Tuathach the first night she stood up to speak. Known for the grain dock and Òrd an t-Seabhaig's twentieth. Told of in: The grain-ships of Ros gheal (SE 24); Òrd an t-Seabhaig's twentieth first paid (SE 24); A fourth coffer from Ros gheal (SE 66).

25.note: A river-island village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig. A town of Oirthir an t-Seabhaig in Siorrachd Cnoc bheag, whose altar Raonaid nic Iain's mother's mother kept before her. In an Cèitean of the thirty-fifth year Òrd an t-Seabhaig met in its hall and named Raonaid custodian of their own by standing up house by house, and Murchadh Ruadh gave her a white feather kept three generations in his house. The letter from Seann Skell refusing to own her was read once in the hall and put away, not burned. Here she wrote Òrd an t-Seabhaig's spoken order into a farm account-book, read it aloud once at the full moon of an t-Samhain, and locked it in the iron box that had held the altar's lamp-oil, wearing the key on a cord under her shawl. The shire's new seal of a white hawk was brought to it in the thirty-sixth year. Known for Òrd an t-Seabhaig's own custodian. Told of in: The Hawk houses' own custodian (SE 35); Òrd an t-Seabhaig gather at Inis ìseal to name a custodian (SE 35); Murchadh Ruadh gives Raonaid the kept feather (SE 35); Seann Skell's letter refusing Raonaid reaches Inis ìseal (SE 35); Òrd an t-Seabhaig carry on as if the custodian had been owned (SE 35); Raonaid nic Iain at Inis ìseal (SE 35).

26.note: A town with a landing of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. A harbour town of the south-west, where Leabhar a' Chùraim of the old vein-house on the hill above the harbour was kept until the house closed it. Eilidh nic Leòid was born here and spent her whole working life in its counting-house and harbour court, copyist, recorder and at last justice in all but name. In the eighth year she was made circuit justice of the south-west and held her first assize here before she had properly left the town, measuring an orchard boundary with knotted cord. She set out from it with Murchadh Clàrc and a satchel of blank record-books, and it was here, within sound of the harbour, that she died in the sixteenth year with the gathered book of her rulings finished on the table by her bed. The fishing villages that feed its market lie along the coast road south from Seann Bhral. Known for Eilidh nic Leòid's town. Told of in: The circuit justices (SE 7); Eilidh nic Leòid's letter of office reaches Cathair dhomhain (SE 7); Eilidh's first assize, held at Cathair dhomhain (SE 7); Eilidh nic Leòid begins the gathered book (SE 15); Eilidh nic Leòid dies (SE 16); Eilidh nic Leòid sends for Uilleam mac Leòid (SE 16).

27.note: A headland harbour of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The harbour below the capital on the lake shore, whose counting-house had come through the war with its shelves whole and whose garrison marched out under terms. In the third year Dùghall mac Iain took the humans' harbour-houses into the kingdom's keeping, and Ailean mac Iain spent eight months copying the humans' tariff out of eleven bound ledgers into Dia-thìris, saying exactly the old thing in the new tongue; the old tariff stood until the mint gave the council coin to take dues in. Its shipwrights took a guild charter in the fourteenth year and its guild court refused a Tuathaich rope-maker's plea in a single sitting. A shipwright of the town was the first name in an Leabharlann's reading-book. Its harbour clerk's corrected copy of Brìghde's crowning proclamation, Niall's name scored through, hangs under glass at the gate. In the thirty-sixth year its eldest masters lost their protest against Ros bheag's coal-ship yard before the guild court. Known for the tariff copied fair, and the proclamation under glass. Told of in: The human counting-houses emptied (SE 2); The Ros dhomhain tariff copied into Dia-thìris (SE 2); Ailean sent to the Ros dhomhain sheds (SE 2); Dùghall mac Iain's reason for copying, not writing anew (SE 2); Ailean's private book begun (SE 2); The harbour-houses of Ros dhomhain taken over (SE 3).

29.note: A large village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. A town of the capital shore. In the twenty-seventh year its glass-houses, which had lately begun blowing small flasks, found a trade no one had planned for them: the women of the town filled the flasks with waters they distilled themselves from bog-myrtle and meadowsweet and heather honey and sold them by the dozen, and within a few years scent was sold in every market town. A cloth trader out of the town, putting in at Cuan shean, offered Harry Marlow a northern passage in the fourteenth year, which Harry refused. Two of its masons drove and cemented the iron reef post at Tobar dhearg for Ciorstaidh nic Artair in the fifty-fifth year, working only the hour either side of the ebb. The glass-houses still stand, and the scent trade still runs from them. Known for the scent-makers' flasks. Told of in: The scent-makers of Seann Vell (SE 27).

30.note: A town of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Headland village with a landing. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The great port south-east of the capital. In the ninth year its shire closed the old burial ground at Cnoc dhìreach to new graves, the vines having split so many stones that no clear plot could be found without turning up someone else's dead. In the fifty-fourth year it opened a covered market over its old strand for the fish that came up from Seann Bhral in the south and from the eastern grounds, the first roof the port had raised over that trade, so that the buyers of the capital could stand dry-shod while they haggled; the strand's old traders grumbled at first and less once a wet winter let them keep a fire by the scales. Known for the covered fish-market. Told of in: Ceann mhin's fish-market (SE 54); Ceann mhin roofs its fish-market (SE 54).

34.note: A village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. A town of the northern coast where Slighe a' Ghuail does not run, whose rope-walks take their hemp from the fields about Doire uaine and Achadh naomh by cart roads older than the survey lines. In the fifty-third year the restored custom chartered its rope-makers as a guild, the last trade the humans never touched to be given a charter of its own. Asked to send the charter south to be filed, the shire keeper answered that it would stay in the shire's own chest, as every paper of the shire had stayed since the chest was locked, and sent south a list of what the chest held and no more. When an Leabharlann called in the shire chests in the sixty-sixth year the old keeper, who had held the key since before Mòrag nic Coinnich was born, burned the chest rather than send it, met the clerks at the gate the next morning with the smoke still on his coat, and paid the council's fine without argument or apology. It is the one shire record of the calling-in an Leabharlann never read. Known for the chest that was burned. Told of in: The rope-makers of Seann Tarr (SE 53); The rope-makers of Seann Tarr chartered (SE 53); Seann Tarr's chest remembered (SE 53); Seann Tarr's chest sends only its list (SE 53); A list is cheaper to lose than a charter (SE 53); The record-chests called in (SE 66).

37.note: A large village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. A town of the north that sent its chest willingly to an Leabharlann in the sixty-seventh year and asked, as no shire before it had, for a copy of everything the chest held to be returned. Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks made the copy, a full transcription bound in the same hand and set beside the original before either left the shire's hall, and the shire's copy became the pattern every later copy an Leabharlann made was cut to. Known for the pattern copy. Told of in: The Seann Toll chest (SE 67); Seann Toll's copy becomes the pattern (SE 67).

38.note: A harbour of Tional nan Tuathach. A Tuathaich fishing harbour of the north coast. On the second night of an t-Sultain in the nineteenth year a westerly drowned eleven men of seven of its boats, Thomas Coyle of Caol mhòr among them; the sea gave back two broken hulls and a stranger's oar. The town had no lifeboat. the lifeboat, white-painted with cork along her gunwales, came up the coast from Cuan shean in an Cèitean of the twentieth year and was put into the water off the town's jetty by that autumn's five widows. Its boats sailed with Mary Coyle to Seann Bhral in the twenty-fifth year, and its fishermen walked to Walter Hale's burial. Known for the eleven drowned, and the lifeboat. 44.note: A farm town of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The town where Rathad na Mèinne from the central mountains comes down to the Abhainn uaine above the gulf. It grew a different way from the pit towns in the twelfth year, taking in carters, inns and a ropewalk, doubling its people within a decade and being given a shire court. Its carters carried the news of the coast south; it was from a carter of the town that Iain Mapa first heard of the raiders off Cathair gheal, third-hand and late. A quarryman of the town put Calum Ruadh down twice in the first hour of the first Còmhrag, and stood over him laughing the second time. Known for Rathad na Mèinne's river crossing. Told of in: Baile thais grows on the coal road (SE 12); Inns and a ropewalk at Baile thais (SE 12); The old boatman's licence at Cidhe Beag (SE 48).

47.note: A large village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The Seann Bhral of the west, on its harbour with the mud flats grey below the town wall and a scorpion carved over the old counting-house door that no one living can account for. Here on the ninth of an t-Sultain in the eighth year Eilidh nic Leòid gave Breith Leòid, that land held under human title passes to An Crùn and the working of it stays with the holders; it was cited in nearly every land case after. The western branch of Slighe a' Ghuail was carried to it in the thirteenth year. Its house of Manannan, reckoned the oldest on the coast, turned away Mary Coyle's eleven boats in the twenty-fifth year: the sea was the same, the house was not. Its fishermen lost the southern grounds to the licence law of the thirtieth year. In the sixty-seventh year the room declined to send its books south to an Leabharlann, and the clerk entered two words, kept north. Known for Tional nan Tuathach, and the two words kept north. The youngest of them, a woman not yet twenty on her first journey south, wrote of it in the school's own minute-book. Seonaid's sentence on the three stones was copied into every school's minute-book from Muileann chiar to this town. Known for the druid houses reopened. In the forty-eighth year the two shires joined their dues to pay for a breakwater across the strait between them, and laid its first stone that spring. It was eight years in the building and is the longest yet built on the island. Known for the shared breakwater. 135.note: A large village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. An Sloc Mòr, the great shaft of the vein: An Crùn's since SE 60, its lowest galleries flooded; Comann nan Gualadairean' town. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The pit town under An Sloc Mòr, at the head of Slighe a' Ghuail. The line was mended through to its pithead in the twelfth year, and the first train out of it had its blessing said over the coal in the first wagon, the old custodian from Muileann dhearg being unwilling to walk the footplate. A quarry was cut above it in the thirteenth year and its dressed stone went south under the Mac Ùisdein wave-mark. Comann nan Gualadairean was chartered in the yard before its pithead on a cold day of an t-Samhain in the thirteenth year, each Dia-thìreach hewer swearing on a lump of coal, its Tuathaich families kept at their work. The guild bound sixty apprentices in its hall after the fall at Muileann dhearg, none of them Tuathaich, and forty households left for the ports that autumn. In the sixty-first year its lowest galleries lay eleven fathoms under water and its three great pumps went south by rail to Seann Bhral's new dry dock. Known for An Sloc Mòr's pithead, the hewers' oath, and the pumps. Its lamp-makers were chartered as a guild in the fourteenth year, and set their mark, a flame struck over a hammer, on every lamp that left their sheds, so that the lamp carried the record of where it was made and under what oath; of all the guild marks the humans' traders had copied this one only. Shaft-lamps were lent from pit to pit after that, and Comann nan Gualadairean kept a minute-book of who lent to whom. Known for the flame over the hammer. 142.note: A hill village of Tional nan Tuathach. A market town of the northern coast, nearer the shire's seat than Baile chrom and twelve miles from it. In the ninth year the north raised here the largest church it had built since An t-Aiseag closed, its stone hauled from a quarry two shires south on carts Tional nan Tuathach paid for by subscription, and in its tower hung the bell of the old chapel at Ros bheag, crated in a barn since the first spring; it rang first on a market morning and carried to the shore road. A thin blessing of the boats was kept here each spring, and after Seann Bhral refused the north in the twenty-fifth year Mary Coyle made it the full Fleadh na Mara: more than fifty boats came on the second Sunday of an Gearran in the twenty-sixth year, blessed with heather dipped in harbour water, and David Hale counted them. Rathad nan Cairtearan runs through it south to Àth fhada. Known for the church of the Ros bheag bell, and Fleadh na Mara. Its fishermen traded in the broken store for two years on their own custom, and in the third year the council granted them a market right for the north-west coast, the smallest clause on Ailean's map of the shires and the one thing on it the town had already made true. Its first maor took the old human magistrate's house, which the town went on calling by its old name. In the fifteenth year Eilidh nic Leòid held her assize here in the heat of an t-Iuchar, heard nineteen causes to their ends and found fifteen for An Crùn; the Coombes and the Pettifers kept their ground on a custodian's countersign. Its timber yard took the order for Àth leathan's props in the thirty-ninth year. Known for the broken lock, and the seventeen suits. A township a little way inland on the south coast, on fields the sea had never in living memory reached, until Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol of the fourth year ran over its low ground and salted in one night what three generations had ploughed. The council moved its survivors to higher ground a mile inland before the winter closed the roads and paid for their seed from the treasury without a due asked, the first relief the restored kingdom granted anyone. The fields lay under salt for a generation. In the twenty-eighth year they bore again, and three households moved away after the wave, or their children in their place, asked for their old ground and were given it; the shire measured them back onto the same strips the humans' surveyors had cut, since those were the bounds the families still walked by memory. The chronicler entered its barley the night before word came of Brìghde's death. Known for the first relief, and the fields that bore again. 160.note: A mill village of Tional nan Tuathach. The mill-town the humans built to watch the northern landing and left to whoever wanted the keeping of it. In the ninth year it was granted a market right for the inland country of the north-west, the second such right any northern town had been given, and the carpenters spent most of a month laying hurdles on the old common green, where mill hands had played ball, to pen the first market's beasts. The Tuathaich drovers of the hill farms, who had walked their stock the long way south, brought them here on set days instead, and from here the droves went on south by the old tracks to Ceann leathan; by midsummer the green stood full every market day and the innkeepers let every room. The vigil-keepers of Oidhche Glaise answered to nobody south of it, and carters driving in from it heard the Cnoc ghorm bell before they saw the tower. Known for the cattle-market on the green. 166.note: A town of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. River-island village with a landing. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. A harbour town of the south-west coast, where the new coin was slower to come than almost anywhere in the kingdom. Its merchants did not wait on the mint: through the sixth year they traded in chits written on the paper of the house of Lia Fàil, whose name was old enough and trusted enough to stand in for coin, and when the coin came the chits were redeemed at the house's door, the house keeping back a tenth. A Ros bheag trader told Walter Hale that a tenth kept back by a name a man trusted was cheaper than a savings box kept by a name he did not. A priest of Òrd na Cloiche of the town heard the first reading of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's written order. Its harbour court was well enough kept that Britheamhan na Cuairte's sitting there in the eighth year was brief. Known for Lia Fàil's chits. Told of in: The coin at Inis thais (SE 6); The house of Lia Fàil's chits redeemed at its door (SE 6); Eilidh's circuit calls at Inis thais (SE 7).

167.note: A hill village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. A shire of the east. On the twenty-first day of an Giblean in the fiftieth year it opened a school in every one of its six parishes, the first shire on the island to do so entire and out of its own dues rather than Tional nan Tuathach's purse or a guild's charity. The last and smallest opened with eleven children and a teacher hired from Baile chiar, who had never taught so few; within two years the benches held twenty and she stayed past her term. The council sent a clerk to ask how a shire so far from its notice had found the coin, and was shown plain accounts in a plain hand, the dues that would have gone to a road never built turned to six rooms and six teachers, and asked nothing further. Known for the six parish schools. Told of in: Cnoc leathan's schools (SE 50); Cnoc leathan's sixth parish school (SE 50).

170.note: A town of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Farm town with a landing. Its people keep the rite of Òrd na Cloiche. A tanning town of the south-west coast. When the panthers crossed the hill country near Baile dhomhain by Imrich nam Pantar in the sixty-second year, its tanners heard of it before the herders had finished counting their losses and sent buyers up into the hills within the fortnight for the hides of the cats the herders' dogs and spears brought down, at a price the herders judged fair. They cured the skins through the summer, and the next year's Fèill Muileann òg saw saddles and belts of panther-hide sold under the town's mark for the first time in any chronicler's memory; the price of the mark doubled twice before the fair's ten days were out. Known for panther-hide under the town's mark. Told of in: The hides of Baile ghorm (SE 62); Baile ghorm's tanners buy the hides (SE 62); Panther-skins first at the fair (SE 62).

174.note: A ford village of Tional nan Tuathach. A Tuathaich village on the old road the north calls Rathad nan Cairtearan, between Cnoc ghorm and the low ground short of Inis àrsaidh. 190.note: A harbour of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. The larger harbour of the south coast struck by Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol in the fourth year. The wave broke its mole and carried its boats inland, so that when Ailean mac Iain came with the relief party the boats of the town lay among the barley and the harbour was gone. Its dead were carried up onto the rise behind the town, above the old harbour line, and buried through that first fortnight in ground the sea had not reached. An Crùn paid a third of the relief, the first time it had paid for anyone's loss. The town righted what boats it could and went back to fishing before the winter closed in. A generation later, in the twenty-seventh year, the harbour was opened again behind a new mole of dressed stone, and of the hulls the wave had cast into the fields one was found sound, caulked, and warped into the new harbour ahead of every boat built for it. Known for the boats in the barley, and the boat kept for a relic. Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain took the house after her first winter's teaching, and in it her students argued the census line for fuil-ghuail by lamplight past the banking of the hearth. Three of them laid on its long table in the forty-ninth year slates copied from Colbh Cnoc chiar, Carragh Cnoc bheag and Calbh Cnoc ghorm, and found a mark like a bent reed and a straight double stroke on all three, which none could read. Catrìona nic Neacail came to teach here in the fifty-seventh year after resigning as surveyor-general, and the bell from Muileann dhearg's shut hall, bought on that shire's vote, rang in the school's tower to call her first lecture. 202.note: A mill village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. A mill town south-east of the capital, where the grain of three shires had gone to be ground since before the humans came, its miller-families' mark cut into a millstone before any shire kept a chest for a charter. In the fifty-third year, with the vein-towns' grain orders thinned by scarce coin, the mills began for the first time in any keeper's memory to grind bark for the tanners of the coast instead of grain, and the families kept their mark and changed the trade under it without asking Comhairle nam Mèinnean's leave. The eldest miller, a woman near seventy, told a passing clerk that a wheel does not know what is under it, and that the grain would come back once the vein-towns had coin to buy it. Known for the mills that turned to bark. In the seventh year its houses were bidden to send witnesses to the settling of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail at Seann Skell; they sent none, and a letter wishing Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail well and promising nothing further, which Dòmhnall mac Thormoid copied onto the first page of his ledger of letters. Òrd na Cloiche kept its own houses, its own mark cut plain over its doors, and its own dealings through the age: it lent coin against a town's dues where a town's need outran a maor's patience, and its paper stood for coin at Inis thais until the coin came. 209.note: A town of Tional nan Tuathach. Agnes Pike's school, Tional nan Tuathach's wool mills, the heart of An Eaglais in the north. Its church is of Eaglais nan Tuathach. An inland town of the northern moss, on rush pasture the settled households were given because the better land nearer the coast was claimed. It buried more of its own in the first hungry winter than any town of the north, and its dead were named on a sheet in the church porch before Tional nan Tuathach had a book to name them in. Meal was carried to it from Caol mhòr on carts that sank to the hubs. In the fifteenth year Agnes Pike opened her school in a widow's byre here, with eleven scholars and no primer but the psalms and Cuimhne-coinneimh an Tionail, and moved it to the church porch each summer; Daniel Frayne walked in to it daily from Muileann leathan. Its weavers wove An Snàthainn Geal, into their cloth, and sold under their own mark from the fifty-fifth year. The wool mills raised here with Tional nan Tuathach's coin turned their first bolt in the fifty-ninth year, and Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's refusal to carry it brought the suit at Seann Bhral. Known for Agnes Pike's byre school and An Snàthainn Geal. 234.note: A mill village of Tional nan Tuathach. Its church is of Eaglais nan Tuathach. A weaving town of the northern moss, close enough across the moor from Doire ghlas that a boy could walk it before the school bell finished. Its householders came to the first sitting of Tional nan Tuathach. Daniel Frayne was a fisherman's son of the town and walked from it daily to Agnes Pike's byre in the fifteenth year; he kept a bindery here from the forty-eighth year on a mended cider-press, teaching young Tuathaich hands a craft the southern guilds would not, and bound Tional nan Tuathach's registers and Muileann shean's primers at his bench. The wool trains of the forty-first year set out from it for Muileann òg by Rathad nan Cairtearan. Clàr nan Leòn was bound here, and its second copy kept at a house in the town that no southern search ever troubled. Frayne, the town's bookbinder and by then Tional nan Tuathach's speaker, carried the Doire ghlas mill's ledgers and Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's refusal to Seann Bhral in the fifty-ninth year and brought home the ruling. Sireadh na Dàrna Fèithe ended on the moor south of it in the fifty-first year, the forty-first shaft striking water at a depth no vein had ever answered. The shafts were left uncovered; sheep fell into them the first winter, and before the next summer was out a child of the town fell into one and was not found until the day after. The parish book holds her name and the day. The shire met in the same low room where it had argued its dues and voted to fence every shaft on its ground at its own cost, post and wire round every mouth, and entered a claim against Taigh Mhic Ùisdein for the fencing that was never paid. Known for the fenced shafts. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. A town east of the mountain, where the town's own custodians had kept rolls and bound books since before An Dealachadh on planks above standing water in a cellar under the old grain-store. In the sixteenth year the council founded an Leabharlann here and named Ailean mac Iain, Ailean Leabhar, its first keeper; the council's minute-books and the humans' tithe ledgers came east to it, the copyists turned its dates into the civil calendar, and its keepers opened Leabhar nan Sloinnidhean, Leabhar nan Aithrisean and Clàr nan Aoisean, counting An Aois Ailein apart. Seanchaidh na Rìoghachd kept her seat here from the eighteenth year rather than at the capital. The town was given a market charter in the seventeenth year, its first fair held in an Leabharlann's yard. Ailean was buried in a small ground behind an Leabharlann in the fortieth year, and Mòrag nic Coinnich kept it thirty years after, calling in the shire chests and building the new wing with its empty fourth floor. A chur san Leabharlann, to put it in an Leabharlann, was first said here. Known for An Leabharlann. 255.note: A hill-fort of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. A walled town of some size on the road east out of Cathair dhearg, its citadel old and its market square older. Oighrig nic Mhathain kept the weighing-scales of its market nine years and caught short weight better-paid men missed, until in the twenty-first year the council's eastern factor made her toll-mistress of the new fair at Muileann òg; she left her scales to a niece she had trained two summers. The carpenters of the town roofed the fair's court, a plain frame open on three sides, a fortnight before the first fair. In am Faoilleach of the twenty-second year the last stretch of the fair's road was metalled past the town, and the toll taken at its gate built a new wall along its southern side by an Lùnastal, which the townsfolk called the fair's wall and the carters called by their own name for the gate. Known for Oighrig's scales, and the fair's wall. 269.note: A hill village of Tional nan Tuathach. A pit town of the western hills, where Tuathaich hewers worked under Comhairle nam Mèinnean's overseers and scales. When the overseers left in the sixty-eighth year with the closing of the Àth leathan branch, the pits passed to the hewers, and they chose to keep the accounts Sam Varley, four-and-fifty, who had kept a private tally beside Comhairle nam Mèinnean's scale for eleven years. He opened a book of the pit's own accounts headed only with the day and the pit's name, the earliest page of the town's register of its pits, and his small son Tom carried the figures between the scale-house and his table. The carters who took Àth leathan's first coal to Seann Bhral by road passed through it. Known for the register of the pits. 273.note: A great farm town of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. A market town on the deep river in the northern hill country. As the coal-towns' trade fell away its market became the market for the wool and hides of the hills, and in the fifty-seventh and fifty-eighth years its market day drew more carts than Fèill Muileann òg, a thing no one living could remember any market doing. A wool-buyer from its hills told Daniel Frayne of it at Tional nan Tuathach's table, and Frayne entered it in the room's ledger under no heading that fit, since it was not Moot business and yet seemed to him to be. Known for the market that passed the fair. Told of in: Baile Mòr dhomhain's market (SE 58).

276.note: A well village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. A village a few miles from an Leabharlann, on the stream below it. In the eighteenth year a family of millers who had not grain enough to keep three wheels busy built a paper-mill here instead, and an Leabharlann's copyists spoke of its first sheets before they had them in hand. Forty quires of its paper went up to Muileann chaol on a borrowed cart, better and cheaper, the copyists judged, than anything the council's stationers had sent, and within the year near enough every sheet an Leabharlann used came from the one stream; nearly every page of Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd in this age is written on its paper. The road east past it smells of wet paper before the mill comes in sight. Known for the paper-mill. 279.note: A field village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. A village on the eastern road where the walkers to the holy well of Allt an Àigh lodge on their way. In the tenth year it was raising a long hall for them, and in the eleventh the hall stood; its keeper, an old woman, wrote each walker's name and shire in a cracked-spined ledger, which held travellers from better than twenty shires that first summer and from fifty by the end of the decade, north and south and east and west of the island together on the one road. The under-clerk Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill lodged here a night with her mother, of an Old Spirits house, on their walk to the well in the tenth year, and thought of the ledger growing a name longer every year while the wall the council had talked of went undrawn. The cairn at the well itself, the keeper told them, grows a little taller every year. Known for the walkers' hall and its ledger. 280.note: A hill village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. A town below the spoil-heaps of old coal galleries, never levelled, on the mountain where the council would not end the working of the vein by day and night. When coal-fuel doubled in price at the fair in the seventieth year, households of the town took to picking coal off the heaps to burn in their own grates, and in the seventy-first year Comhairle nam Mèinnean posted watchmen over the heaps. The watchmen were men of the town, and every night of the posting they saw nothing, though the heaps grew lower and the poorer grates burned warmer than the fair's price could have bought. Known for the watchmen who saw nothing. Told of in: The night-shift kept (SE 11); Coal thieves at Cnoc fhiadhaich (SE 71); The watchmen at Cnoc fhiadhaich see nothing (SE 71).

282.note: A harbour of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The harbour of the west coast where the first humans came ashore generations before. Households were walked north out of it under guard in the first year. An Sireadh sailed from it on the eleventh of an t-Ògmhios in the third year under Aonghas mac Mhurchaidh, a Cuan shean man, to seek An t-Aiseag north-about. Seumas Crùbach kept his shipwright's yard here, building frame first, and took Harry Marlow of Doire mhin on as a bound apprentice; when the guild charter reached the coast in the fourteenth year he tore the boy's indenture and kept him as a free hand at half wage, and other yards took up the rate. Harry measured a derelict human hull on the hard in his own book. The Cuan bheag lifeboat was built in its yard. Known for the first landing-stone, and Harry Marlow's torn indenture. 297.note: A town of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. A town of the southern plain. In the thirty-third year An Crùn's grain-store here was finished, two winters building and one summer roofing, a hall of dressed stone long enough that a loaded cart could turn inside it, great enough to feed the south a season, filled from the south's own harvests. It opened its doors first in a poor season that same year, and in the forty-third it fed the dry country about Achadh shean, its grain reaching the sidings there by Slighe a' Ghuail on the morning of the first rain. In the sixty-third year the harvest came in so thick that the maor wrote to Muileann chaol of granaries built for a lean year wanting a second storey, and Tormod Pinn struck through his own note of a hungry year to come. Known for An Crùn's grain-store. 304.note: A ford village of Tional nan Tuathach. A town an easy day's ride from Caol mhòr, seat of a northern shire. Its maor's chest was the one the northern shires filled for the first chronicle circuit in the nineteenth year, and Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill found in it the maor's returns and nothing more, not a line in a Tuathaich hand, and wrote the fact down without a further word. Eachann mac Rath practised physic here twenty years under his guild's charter. In the thirty-fourth year he took Ruth Ashby and Clara Tulloch, two women of the fishing country, to learn by watching him set bones and mix poultices through a fever season; a factor's wife let slip at a fair stall that his new girls handled a lancet as steady as he did, and the guild struck him from its rolls. He kept his surgery open all the same. Known for the Tuathaich doctors. 305.note: A town of Tional nan Tuathach: the town of Oidhche Glaise vigil, kept indoors since the magistrate's fine. Its church is of Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise. A scatter of grey houses above a shingle beach where the coast turns, its nets strung to dry on frames mended every spring with the fathers' twine. It kept one of Fàinne nan Teintean-rabhaidh on the capes, whose keeper wrote on the first morning of the age that no ship came. Its small church in a net-store answered to the same distant bishops as the great one at Cnoc ghorm. In the ninth year the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane kept Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise in the open on the headland below the old light, as no keeper had kept it before; the bishops called it irregular in a letter that stayed folded behind the altar-cloth. The magistrate fined her for it in the twenty-seventh year, Tional nan Tuathach paid the fine, and the vigil went into a lent byre. In the seventeenth year the town's light was given a Dia-thìreach keeper under a warrant bidding him report what he saw by land as well as by sea, and in the thirty-second year he reported the vigil kept silent in the tower's shadow; the council answered nothing. Known for Oidhche Glaise on the headland, and the fifth light. 324.note: A town of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Grove village with a landing. Its people keep the rite of Òrd na Cloiche. A harbour town of the south-west on the road between Cathair dhomhain and Seann Bhral, where Eilidh nic Leòid's circuit passed. A grave-list from the town was among the first papers the chronicler copied fair, and a wedding there went into Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd beside Brìghde's death. In the thirtieth year it built its own harbour, the first raised anywhere in the kingdom since An Dealachadh without a coin of An Crùn's in it, the house of Òrd na Cloiche lending against the town's dues and the masons building the mole to Òrd na Cloiche's measure; the house took its first quarter's dues off the quay before the last course was dry. A fishing boat of the town struck the reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg in the fifty-fourth year, and the keeper Artair mac Mhurchaidh drowned bringing in her crew; the town's fishing families paid half the reef bell that followed. Known for the harbour built on Lia Fàil's loan. 326.note: A mill village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Bhrìde. The southernmost of Òrd an t-Seabhaig's houses, close by the coast and far south of Cnoc bheag. It did not wait on the reading: in the sixth year it sent word to Seann Skell that it would take Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's written order entire, whatever it proved to be, and hung in its doorway a bell cast new for the purpose, the first bell any hawk-house had hung, to ring at Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's measured burnings. It rang it that summer at the burning of the year before a small crowd in the lane. Dòmhnall mac Thormoid wrote to it in his own hand, the first letter of thanks he composed in his office, and sent it a last copy of the order made with more care than any other. It became a house of Òrd Bhrìde, the one hawk-house of its kind. Known for the first bell hung in a hawk-house. 330.note: A village of Tional nan Tuathach. River-island village with a landing. A town of the north-western coast whose harbour officers sailed with the last ships and took their keys with them. In the second year its people opened the locked harbour store after Ceann mhòr and Cathair gheal did, and it is told that three women of the town drew up a reckoning of what was taken and by whom, so that the sharing could be answered for if anyone ever came to ask; no maor came. The old Rathad nan Cairtearan runs down to it from Cnoc ghorm and Àth fhada, and the wool trains of the forty-first year crossed the flooded low ground short of it in a cold rain, the carts finding their own way round the water. A household at a crossing near it kept one of the three lamps that lit the road by night. In the fifty-third year An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn pitched on the common near the town, and its magistrate licensed the acts as various, the fee paid. Known for the three women's reckoning, and An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn licensed as various. 346.note: A ford village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. A gathering of pits and shanties in the western hills where Tuathaich hewers had worked the coal since before the kingdom drew a road to them. In the thirteenth year Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn built a spur of thirteen miles to it off the western branch, because the coal was cheap to lift and the carters' road worse each winter. After the fall at Muileann dhearg Comhairle nam Mèinnean's new timbering rule was posted on its pit-head door and the timber ordered from Ceann mhòr, and the timber never came; the hewers went on under the old props, and Mary Coyle named the town in her letter to Comhairle nam Mèinnean. In the sixty-eighth year Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn shut the branch and Comhairle nam Mèinnean withdrew its overseers, and the pits passed to the hewers, who chose captains, weighed every cart and set by An Crùn's fifth under Breith Leòid; Comhairle nam Mèinnean entered the payments as arrears. Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's factors at its railhead, the nearest to the north, refused the Doire ghlas mill's cloth in the fifty-ninth year and weighed its first bale onto the line in the sixtieth. From the sixty-ninth year its coal went to Seann Bhral by cart. Known for the pits the hewers kept. 354.note: A large village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr: the shunting yards of Slighe a' Ghuail and the rows of the yard families. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The shunting town where the line from An Sloc Mòr meets the older line down to the ports. The council mended Slighe a' Ghuail as far as it in the eighth year and no further, and the humans' own timetable, copied fair, was hung on a board at its terminus. Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn laid new sidings here in the thirteenth year, and the shunting families, who had worked the humans' small engines, were counted apart on a roll of their own and housed in the rows nearest the lines; in the twenty-fourth year the rows had more children born than they had cradles for, among them Seachran and Brean. Calum mac Aonghais, called Calum Ruadh, a hewer of the town, won the first Còmhrag. In the sixty-third year its yard families stopped the coal trains three days over a cut wage, with Dòmhnall Ruadh mac Ailein as their spokesman; the wage was restored and eleven men dismissed. Known for the shunting rows and the stopped trains. 364.note: A hill village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. A small town low on its shingle on the south coast, which gave its name to Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol of the fourth year, Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol. The water broke it in a single night before running on to Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin. It was built again the following spring on the slope behind its old ground, high enough that the sea would have to climb a hill to trouble it a second time, and the old site was left as the water left it; the townsfolk call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, and do not build there. Its shepherds and those of Ros gharbh had summered their flocks time out of mind on the low island of Eilean mhin offshore, over which the wave also passed. Its houses were raised again faster than Ros gharbh's boats, a house wanting only hands and a boat wanting a builder. Known for the wave's name, and an Tràigh Bhàthte. Told of in: Cnoc chaol rebuilt on the hill (SE 4).

365.note: A great farm town of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. The market town of the middle country, seat of its own shire. Its courthouse burned in the last summer of the war, and when Coinneach mac Ailein, a custodian's younger son, came as its first maor in the fourth year he held his court under the market roof among the fish-scales. When a new courthouse was raised two years on he sat in it for exactly one sitting and moved back to the market hall the week after, and the two maoir who followed him did the same, until holding court under the scales became simply how justice was done in the town and no one thought to write down why. Ailean mac Iain had ridden no further north than its market before An Dealachadh, and he rode its letters to it again when the maoir were named. Its roll of arms and its dues were entered in the fourth year with the rest of the kingdom's. Known for the court held under the market roof. 411.note: A field village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. A shire of the drove road where the ground failed once before in the humans' time and was given a name for it that its people never forgot, Tiormachd Achadh shean, the drought of the old field. In the forty-third year the rains of am Màrt held off into an Cèitean and the wells of the drove road went brackish and then, three of them, dry to the stone. Its maor, a careful man who kept his own tally, wrote south before the second month of the dry was out, holding that a man argues with a poor harvest but a well gone to stone argues with no one, and cut twelve new wells along the road, one of them dry from the day it was dug on a dowser's word. The council answered faster than the north had ever known it to answer: grain from An Crùn's store at Cathair fhada reached the town's sidings by Slighe a' Ghuail on the morning the first proper rain fell. 422.note: A hill-fort of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. A town of the hill and moor country where Sireadh na Dàrna Fèithe began. In the fifty-first year the first of Alasdair mac Ùisdein's shafts went down on the rise above it in stone that gave every hopeful sign, and was judged barren within the fortnight; a dozen of the forty-one dry shafts were sunk on its hills. An old digger of the town, who had cut peat there as a boy, told Catrìona nic Neacail that the shepherds called the ground am Fearann Falamh. In the fifty-second year the town brought its claim for spoiled grazing to the circuit court, two shepherds swearing that the search cost them more lambs in two years than wolves had in ten, and the court found for the town; Taigh Mhic Ùisdein let its stone hall to meet the damages. A Holy Age survey in an Leabharlann had named the same hills searched and barren long before. Known for the first of the forty-one shafts. 476.note: A town of Tional nan Tuathach. A walled town of the north-west coast, its harbour a shallow bay below the town wall. In the second year its people loosed the humans' locked loft of nets to every boat in the harbour on a single tide. From the twelfth year ships flying no flag worked its waters; a fishing house was burned below the town and two boats taken, and the council's minute asked that the matter be watched. In the twentieth year Nell Barrow, a skipper's widow, wrote twice to the council for a boat or leave to arm its own and was answered by neither letter. On the night of 8 an Giblean three flagless hulls stood into the bay; the largest ran onto a shifted bar and was boarded and burned by seven town boats before dawn, at a cost of two dead and four hurt. The council fined the town four purses of Bonn na Rìoghachd for bearing arms without leave, and Walter Hale carried Tional nan Tuathach's share of it north; the fine was counted out at the maor's door. Known for the bay cleared, and the fine paid. 489.note: A city of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The humans' great harbour of the west, on the coast below the capes, where the fishing fleets still came in under a flag they had never learned to read and the old harbour bell rang the hours by a humans' clock. In the second year Ailean mac Iain found in its counting-house eleven district surveys behind a locked grating, every field about the town walked and numbered, and boxed them apart for the council; from them the shires were drawn. An Sireadh came home to its quay in the third year after sixteen days north-about and no land, and the priests of Manannan said over her return the prayer they had said over her going, that the sea be kept shut. Its innkeeper told Ailean of Niall's crowning. The ship lay careened here that winter. It is not the Seann Skell of the southern coast, where Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's Àrd-choimheadaiche sits, and the record keeps the two apart as west and south. Known for the district surveys, and An Sireadh's berth. 491.note: A large village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr: the vein-town that doubled in the first years and has lost a third of its households to the ports; its druid hall shut and its bell sold. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. A town of narrow streets and spoil-stone chapels five miles from the great shaft, grown fat on An Sloc Mòr's overflow and working its own pits to keep the greater mine's yield steady. It took the most of the hungry families who came to the vein in the twelfth year, and its old druid hall was cut into lodgings over ground Comhairle nam Mèinnean had to mark as sound or not. Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's house here sent the old custodian who blessed the first train. It sent the largest company to the first Còmhrag. The Cill ghlas district under it, shut since Scàineadh Cill ghlas of the humans' time, was reopened by Comhairle nam Mèinnean; on the first day of an t-Iuchar in the thirty-ninth year its galleries fell and thirty-one men died, and they were buried in a single ground at the edge of the town's yard, the custodian reading over each grave. By the fifty-seventh year its maor counted above sixty houses empty; its Fèidh hall, given back to Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, was locked by its last teacher, and its bell sold to Caol shean. Known for the fall of the thirty-one. 492.note: A ford village of Rìoghachd Dia-thìr. A salt town on the tidal flats of the east coast below Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, worked by Dia-thìreach ford-keepers, its boats crewed as often by Tuathaich hands as not. Its flats were dug for salt-pans in the thirty-second year and it was soon supplying salt up the coast. In an Gearran of the forty-fourth year flagless ships came in under cloud and burned its three salt-sheds; the patrol came two days late, and the households judged the captain's honest report an accounting that answered every question but the one that mattered. The sheds were raised again within the year, An Crùn paying a third. Mòrag nic Coinnich was made an Leabharlann's deputy on the road home from it. Known for the salt-sheds burned, and the raiders named. 14.note: One of the five lights, burning coal-lit flame; Dia-thìreach keepers by royal warrant. Told of in: The keepers of the five lights (SE 17).

15.note: One of the five lights, burning coal-lit flame; Dia-thìreach keepers by royal warrant. Told of in: The keepers of the five lights (SE 17).

16.note: One of the five lights, burning coal-lit flame; Dia-thìreach keepers by royal warrant. Told of in: The keepers of the five lights (SE 17); The drowned lighthouse keeper (SE 54); Ciorstaidh nic Artair's reef mark (SE 55).

34.note: Founded SE 16; Ailean Leabhar, then Mòrag nic Coinnich, then Raghnall mac Mhuirich keepers; enlarged SE 67. Told of in: Leabharlann Muileann chaol founded (SE 16); Ailean Leabhar, first keeper (SE 16); Mòrag nic Coinnich, keeper (SE 40); The library enlarged (SE 67); Raghnall mac Mhuirich, keeper (SE 70).

35.note: Recorded SE 53 on the common near Inis àrsaidh. Told of in: The Circus at Inis àrsaidh (SE 53).

36.note: First recorded SE 25 near Seann Chwen. Told of in: The circus at Seann Chwen (SE 25).

37.note: First fought SE 23; edged tools banned SE 54; its greatest crowd SE 45, won by Ealasaid nic Coinnich. Told of in: Còmhrag Ceann leathan first fought (SE 23); The Còmhrag at its height (SE 45); Edged tools banned from the Còmhrag (SE 54).

38.note: The fair first held SE 21 under Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules; the northern day SE 55; the coal price doubled SE 70. Told of in: Fèill Muileann òg first held (SE 21); Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules (SE 21); The Fèill's northern day (SE 55); The coal price at the fair (SE 70).

41.note: Closed to new graves by the shire of Ceann mhin (SE 9). Told of in: The necropolis at Cnoc dhìreach (SE 9).

add.name: An Sloc Mòr
add.note: The great shaft: An Crùn's concession to Mac Ùisdein, then An Crùn's alone; its lowest galleries flooded; its great pumps sold to Seann Bhral. Told of in: The Sloc Mòr concession (SE 11); The Crown's share of the Sloc Mòr (SE 60); The Sloc Mòr's pumps (SE 61); The pumps sold (SE 62).

add.name: the boundary stones on the north roads
add.note: Set where the Tuathaich country begins; no wall follows them. Told of in: The boundary stones set (SE 1); The border wall proposed (SE 10).

add.name: An Tràigh Bhàthte
add.note: The old site of Cnoc chaol, left as Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol left it; no one builds there. Told of in: Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol (SE 4); Cnoc chaol rebuilt on the hill (SE 4).

add.name: the mint
add.note: In the old human counting-house; each coin's seal pressed with ink of coal dust. Told of in: The old human coinage withdrawn (SE 5); The mint at Cathair dhearg (SE 5).

add.name: the forty-one dry shafts
add.note: Sireadh na Dàrna Fèithe, from the hills above Dùn dhearg to the moors south of Baile ruadh; the same hills were searched and barren in An Aois Naomh. Told of in: The search for a second vein (SE 51); Forty-one dry shafts (SE 51); The shafts at Baile ruadh left open (SE 52).

add.name: the fall at Muileann dhearg
add.note: Thirty-one hewers dead along a line marked sound: the same fault as Scàineadh Cill ghlas. Told of in: The fall at Muileann dhearg (SE 39).

add.name: the church at Cnoc ghorm
add.note: The greatest church in the north and its school; the northern feast of the boats. Told of in: The churches of the north (SE 9); The church school at Cnoc ghorm (SE 10); The northern sea-feast (SE 26).

add.name: Tional nan Tuathach
add.note: Tuathaich householders and their speaker; minutes unbroken since the first meeting. Told of in: The Moot at Caol mhòr (SE 2).

add.name: the market cross of Mac Ùisdein
add.note: The house's name on all four faces; the wool and coal markets moved to its foot. Told of in: The market cross at Cathair mhòr (SE 20).

add.name: the ancestors' hall of Seann Dunn
add.note: Forty families name their ancestors aloud each year. Told of in: The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn (SE 22).

add.name: Breith Leòid
add.note: Land held by Tuathaich under human title passes to An Crùn; the right to work it stays with the holders. Told of in: The Leòid ruling (SE 8); The Seann Bhral ruling (SE 59).

add.name: the waterworks of Muileann bhàn
add.note: The first public waterworks of the kingdom. Told of in: Muileann bhàn's waterworks (SE 8).

add.name: the copper workings of Àth fhiadhaich
add.note: Not the vein; the town's Seann Spioradan house gives them no blessing. Told of in: The copper at Àth fhiadhaich (SE 60); Àth fhiadhaich's copper-town (SE 61).

add.name: Ciorstaidh nic Artair's reef post
add.note: An iron post on the reef, painted and hung with a bell. Told of in: The drowned lighthouse keeper (SE 54); Ciorstaidh nic Artair's reef mark (SE 55).

add.name: the lifeboat of Cuan bheag
add.note: Bought by Tional nan Tuathach's subscription after eleven fishermen drowned; the council paid a third. Told of in: Boats lost off Cuan bheag (SE 19).

50.note: The fair road from Cathair dhearg to Muileann òg, widened and metalled for the carts of the fair; Dùn chrom takes a toll at its gate. Told of in: The fair's road (SE 21).

383.note: The cold way of the north coast, laid up in LE 1,634. Told of in: Inis mhòr's grain fleet laid up (LE 1,634).

385.note: The pilgrims' boats of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail from the southern Seann Skell round to Caol naomh.

add.name: Slighe a' Ghuail
add.note: Mended as far as Muileann chrom (SE 8) and carried up the valley to An Sloc Mòr (SE 12); Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's sidings at Muileann chrom. Told of in: The coal line repaired (SE 8); The coal line reaches the Sloc Mòr (SE 12); The shunting yards at Muileann chrom (SE 13).

add.name: the western branch of Slighe a' Ghuail
add.note: West from Cathair dhearg to the port of Seann Bhral (SE 13); its spur north to the pits at Àth leathan was shut in SE 68. Told of in: The western branch (SE 13); The branch line to Àth leathan closed (SE 68).

add.name: Slighe a' Ghuail to Ceann leathan
add.note: Carried through to the port so coal may ship from a second harbour (SE 36). Told of in: The coal line reaches Ceann leathan (SE 36).

add.name: Rathad nan Cairtearan
add.note: The carters of the northern wool go to the fair by Cnoc ghorm, Àth fhada and the old road down to Inis àrsaidh; the Tuathaich villages on the way open inns. In the south it has no name. Told of in: The Tuathaich wool carts (SE 40); The Tuathaich carters' road (SE 41).

add.name: the eastern salt drove road
add.note: The salt of Àth bheag goes inland by the old drove road past Baile ìseal. Told of in: Salt-pans of Àth bheag (SE 32).
The way Niall came. Told of in: A saying enters speech (SE 3).
To put it in an Leabharlann. Told of in: A chur san Leabharlann (SE 16).

4.note: Cnoc chaol, Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin laid waste in one night; a little over forty dead; the wave ran up the gulf to Ros gharbh. Told of in: Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol (SE 4); The dead of the Great Wave counted (SE 4); Achadh mhin under salt (SE 4); The wave's reach on Eilean mhin (SE 5).

2.note: Grain sent up Slighe a' Ghuail; no one died of hunger; twelve wells dug along the drove road. Told of in: Dry years at Achadh shean (SE 43); The wells of Siorrachd Achadh shean (SE 43); Grain by the coal line (SE 44).

3.note: Declared safe; new shafts well back from the old fault line. Told of in: The Cill ghlas district reopened (SE 15); The fall at Muileann dhearg (SE 39).

add.name: Tìr-dhùthchais nan Tuathach
add.note: Fixed by law; a confinement, yet their children's children call it home. Told of in: The Tuathaich homeland fixed (SE 1); The boundary stones set (SE 1).

add.name: an Oirthir Ghaothach
add.note: The shire lines stop at the great moss where the humans' survey stopped; sealers, fowlers and herders, uncounted. Told of in: The windy coast left out (SE 3).

add.name: An Traoghadh: the vein's last unworked stretches (SE 56)
add.note: Catrìona nic Neacail's map fits on one sheet. Told of in: The Depletion first noted (SE 26); Iain Mapa's survey (SE 26); The Depletion laid bare (SE 56); Catrìona nic Neacail's map (SE 56).

add.name: the stone's shires (their own count, SE 65)
add.note: Òrd na Cloiche publish a count of their people that agrees with the kingdom's within a hundred. Told of in: The census in the Stone's shires (SE 65).

add.name: the panthers' host (SE 62)
add.note: A great host of panthers crosses the south-west near Baile dhomhain. Told of in: The panthers cross the south-west (SE 62); Imrich nam Pantar in the chronicle (SE 62).

add.name: an Tràigh Bhàthte
add.note: Ground the sea has taken. Told of in: Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol (SE 4); Cnoc chaol rebuilt on the hill (SE 4).

add.name: An Sloc Mòr
add.note: Ground the sea has taken. Told of in: The Sloc Mòr's pumps (SE 61).
